record.paper_title: Homogenization in mechanics. A survey of solved and open problems
record.original_question: For thermoelastic composite bodies, how should homogenization describe local stress and strain fields, local material properties, and nonlinear effects such as plasticity, fracture, or irreversible damage when thermal loading can create nonzero local stress even if the macroscopic boundary is free and the temperature is later returned to zero?

evidence.quote: much work is to be done

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a thermoelastic composite body occupying a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$, composed of two or more constituents arranged on a microscale of characteristic length $\varepsilon$ that is much smaller than the macroscopic dimensions of $\Omega$. Each constituent is assumed to obey a local constitutive law that combines linear thermoelasticity with possible nonlinear effects, namely:
(i) elasto-plastic response with a yield criterion and hardening law,
(ii) progressive damage characterized by an internal scalar or tensorial damage variable, and
(iii) brittle fracture along internal interfaces.
The body is subjected to a prescribed temperature field $T(x,t)$ which varies in time and returns to its reference value $T \equiv 0$ at the final time; the macroscopic boundary $\partial \Omega$ is left traction-free, and no external body forces are applied. Owing to mismatch of thermal expansion coefficients between constituents, the microscopic stress and strain fields may remain nonzero (residual stresses, residual plastic strains, and accumulated damage) even after the temperature has been restored.

Develop a rigorous homogenization theory that, in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$, produces:
(a) effective (macroscopic) constitutive relations linking macroscopic stress, strain, temperature, and internal variables for the composite, accounting for the three nonlinear mechanisms above;
(b) a reconstruction (localization) procedure that recovers, from the macroscopic fields, the local stress and strain fields together with the local material state (plastic strain, damage, crack distribution) inside a representative volume element; and
(c) a characterization of the residual local stress/strain state that persists after a thermal loading-unloading cycle returning the temperature to zero, including conditions on microstructure and constituent properties that guarantee existence, uniqueness, and stability of the homogenized evolution.
artifact.category_tag: homogenization of thermoelastic composites with nonlinear dissipation
artifact.status_search_result: The literature contains many partial results: computational and mean-field homogenization schemes for thermo-elastoplastic composites, reduced-order models for temperature-dependent thermoelasticity, finite-volume micromechanics for ratcheting with thermal residual stresses, and nonlinear viscoelastic/viscoplastic constitutive frameworks with damage. However, a unified rigorous homogenization theory that simultaneously handles thermoelasticity, plasticity, damage, and fracture with full local field reconstruction and residual-stress characterization after thermal cycling remains an active area with no complete solution; the topic continues to be treated as an open problem in surveys of homogenization in mechanics.

status_evidence.title: Homogenization and thermoelastic analysis of heterogeneous materials with regular and random microstructures
status_evidence.snippet: Effective properties and microscopic thermal stresses are estimated for thermoelastic composites with regular and random microstructures.
status_evidence.claim: Partial progress exists on local thermal stress evaluation via homogenization.

status_evidence.title: A thermo-elastoplastic self-consistent homogenization method for inter-granular plasticity with application to thermal ratcheting of TATB
status_evidence.snippet: Self-consistent homogenization for thermo-elastoplastic polycrystals applied to thermal ratcheting.
status_evidence.claim: Plasticity coupled with thermal loading has been treated in special homogenization settings, but not in full generality with damage and fracture.

status_evidence.title: Homogenization and Localization of Ratcheting Behavior of Composite Materials and Structures with the Thermal Residual Stress Effect
status_evidence.snippet: Finite-volume direct averaging micromechanics is extended to study ratcheting under thermal residual stress.
status_evidence.claim: Localization and residual thermal stress effects are studied numerically; a complete rigorous theory including damage and fracture is not provided.

status_evidence.title: Reduced order homogenization of thermoelastic materials with strong temperature dependence
status_evidence.snippet: Reduced-order computational homogenization for strongly temperature-dependent thermoelastic composites.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work addresses temperature-dependent thermoelastic homogenization but does not resolve coupled plasticity/damage/fracture in full.
